🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His focus is on removing those barriers so engineers, designers, and product teams can speak honestly, make decisions, and take ownership of their work.

He makes intent explicit, pushes decisions to the people closest to the work, and uses transparency and direct feedback. He coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. His non-negotiables include psychological safety, integrity and respect, continuous learning, and “outcomes, not optics.” He also chooses environments where intensity is balanced with respect for people.

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, that included a “permit to fail” learning environment. Teams had avoided risks because they feared blame. Matt introduced non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. Instead of pointing fingers, teams applied lessons to subsequent sprints. In innovation work, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail: the goal was to test assumptions before committing to costly builds.

He also built balanced teams with engineers, product managers, and UX architects sharing accountability, rather than working through hierarchical handoffs. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and open feedback gave people ways to share knowledge and change how they worked.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also reduced project delays, improved retention, and achieved **zero-defect production code**.

Matt’s work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement: shipping enterprise platforms, changing how teams build software, and building the engineering organization itself.

Many new hires also lacked hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies and modern engineering practices. Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, with full P&L accountability, hiring, training, and career development.

Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, exposed vague backlog stories, and brought in TDD experts to work alongside the team. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Across CIC engagements, teams achieved **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. At **JP Morgan Chase**, teams outpaced peer velocity within the first **2 sprints**, shipping production code in weeks rather than months. The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients** and contributed to **\$100M+ in repeat business** through delivery excellence and customer relationships.

answer_md:
🐾 Matt’s account of a failure centers on assumptions he did not verify.

He was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. Identity and access management (IAM) controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not validate access patterns, audit who could trigger downstream email processes, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. Data masking and email interception were not in place as compensating controls.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The human consequence was explicit: the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” and said leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

His stated change afterward was to make IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities, rather than treating inherited configurations as verified facts.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured program that would prepare engineers for cloud-native projects, not just certification exams.

As Cloud Native Architecture Lead, Matt led AWS Launchpad in collaboration with AWS from **July 2018** to **November 2019**. He designed structured learning paths covering AWS core services, including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate, alongside cloud-native application development.

Instead of relying on theory, he delivered interactive workshops and hands-on labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments. The learning paths connected certification preparation with practical application, so engineers worked with the technologies they would use on cloud transformation projects.

Matt also established cloud expert mentorship teams to share best practices and build institutional knowledge. He organized group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops, giving participants support beyond individual study. The program combined structured coursework, practical exercises, and access to experienced cloud practitioners rather than treating certification as a standalone training event.

More than **200 professionals** earned AWS certifications, including AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer. The program accelerated cloud adoption across **Accenture** and the launch of cloud-native initiatives, while establishing ongoing mentorship and knowledge sharing across teams.
